item.title: A Term for a Kind of Human Economic Obsolescence?
item.description:
AI keeps getting more capable. At some point, likely in the next 1-3 years unless we do something to stop it, we get to where AI systems are able to do everything almost anyone can do. This is often described as leading to a world with "no jobs", but I think this tends to confuse more than help.

One sense in which there might be no jobs is that there might be no people. This is a very real concern, [1] and is the primary reason I think we need to slow down or pause AI development, but isn't what I'm trying to talk about here.

Instead, when people say "no jobs", they're usually talking about a future where there are still people but humans are basically never the best way to go from "I have money" to "my problem is solved". The history of automation has had many rounds of taking some kinds of problem and moving it to machines or human-directed machines: almost all ketchup bottles are filled by machines, almost all dirt is moved by human-controlled machines. As long as there were other things that needed doing which humans could do better than machines, though, humans have moved into other lines of work, and the futures envisioned by a 1930 Keynes in Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren haven't come about. But this is changing fast, as the list of things we can do better than machines rapidly shrinks.

Words like "no jobs" or "economically obsolete" don't really apply in these futures, though, since I do still expect people to pay others to do things. When you go to a concert and close your eyes listening to a fantastic performance, there's a sense in which the performer is obsolete: the PA system could be (and sometimes is) putting out a recording instead of music live in the moment. But we care that there is a person up there entertaining us. People buy handmade things (or are tricked into thinking they are), and enjoy receiving services from people.

So I'd like some better terms for this potential world in which nothing humans do feeds into whether anyone is fed, has shelter, gets medical care, or has any other basic need met, but where people still do things for each other, sometimes for pay, because of a preference that some portions be done by a human. Thoughts? I asked Opus 5.5, and its favorite phrasing was (sigh) "non-load-bearing".


[1] The people building the models do not know how to reliably control them or how much we should trust them. As much as there is a plan, it's to almost entirely delegate resolving this problem to these same models we don't know how to control and don't know how much to trust. Here's Kelsey Piper writing after a visit to Anthropic:

The public is hotly debating whether AI is a normal technology — something that will transform our world like the internet did — or more like the arrival of postindustrial modernity to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the 1950s: something that vaporized a culture overnight. The third option is that AI is more like the rise of humanity as seen from the perspective of livestock animals. (In this scenario, AIs are the humans, and we are the animals whose fate will make no sense to us.)

Anthropic believes that the second possibility is already baked in, and it's hoping to prevent the third — but its plan for preventing that looks more like hope and guesswork than something we should trust it with.



Discuss

item.title: Data as particles and mean field theory abound
item.description:
Epistemic status: Much of this post is a reframing of known results using slightly different tooling. The framing of "data as particles" has been conceptually useful for me so it seemed useful to share. Some steps in the derivations are stated and handwaved rather than writing out in full where the steps are generally standard. The dynamical mean field perspective presented later is part of a broader research agenda, and a paper deriving more formal results about it will be out soon!

Author Note: The automated LLM written detection really wanted to consider this post as LLM written. So maybe putting this at the start will help. This is not written in any substantial way by an LLM. It might be slop, but it is human generated slop.

Introduction

Very early in my machine learning career I worked on group equivariant neural networks. These for a while became the dominant kind of neural networks in things molecular property prediction with the early advent of things like Schnet. This, through a series of events pulled me into the world of the quantum many body problem, and then into a quantum chemistry lab, where I would do my PhD (though not technically in quantum chemistry). This corrupted me though, because suddenly everything started to look like a many body problem.

Such a perspective though has lead to some nice insights, and I think it offers a way of reframing some results in learning theory in a way that opens up some new tools or ways of thinking about learning. In particular, I have found it useful for studying learning under gradient based optimizers, and thought other people might find it useful as well. While more formal research papers building around what is in this blog post are coming, I think the nature of formal research papers tends to make the core takeaways and intuition somewhat obscure. This post attempts to alleviate some of this by being a bit more pedagogical. There are a few sections which can be summarized as follows:

  • We explain how one can think of datapoints as particles, and the model parameters as defining bonds between them.
  • Using this perspective, we derive a mean field theory of the data, and show that this leads naturally to the Bayesian free energy of singular learning theory.
  • We show how one gets a dynamical mean field theory of the data when considering the behaviour of SGD in the large data/small learning rate limit.
  • Taking this perspective, we show that the dynamical mean field theory is effectively second order, and relate this to the static mean field of singular learning theory.

This post does get a little mathematically dense in places. We do try and make it somewhat more legible for those unfamiliar with mean field theory/many body physics though!

Bonds between datapoints

In some sense the starting point for this is the simplest object in machine learning: the loss function. For a model with parameters and (for pedagogy) let's consider a finite dataset with the drawn i.i.d. from some data distribution , so the empirical loss becomes

with the population loss defined via the standard limit.

One thing about the loss that sometimes goes underappreciated is that it looks a lot like what we might call a "parametrized Hamiltonian". To see this note that we can read the empirical loss as a total energy written as a sum of energies of individual "particles" in the system. Each datapoint is a particle, and is its energy when the model has parameters .

Notice that every particle shares the same . To see why this is important imagine a black box with three lightbulbs on top who are wired in some unknown way, whose brightness reports the energies , , , and a panel of twenty unlabeled knobs. We know nothing about what the knobs do, but we want to understand how the lightbulbs are wired. Now imagine we start twisting the knobs and just seeing what they do. Knob 7 brightens A and B a little and dims C. Knob 12 brightens all three by different amounts. Knob 3 mostly does something to C. This is kind of messy, hard to interpret exactly what each knob does. So we start just kind of going nuts, twisting and turning the knobs in random ways and looking at the outputs. We sort of ignore exactly what knobs do what, and just kind of see how the lightbulbs change together. Looking at the bulb, one can see that maybe changes which change A are very likely to change B, maybe C always dims if both A and B brighten, etc. So we may not know exactly what each knob does, but we can kind of infer how strongly each bulb is wired to each other bulb

We can pretty simply put some math to this for the loss. Starting with the simple "two body" story, imagine we perturb and for simplicity just take . The bond between two particles is the covariance of their energies under this perturbation:

A kind of nice result (that will become useful later) is that if we Taylor expand this then to first order, with which gives an approximation of the covariance like:

Averaging over random perturbations sums out the parameter index , leaving you with indices in the data space, so the parameters are exactly what gives the relationships between particles.

Beyond pairwise bonds

The above construction only captures two-body structure. It tells us whether two datapoints tend to respond together if we perturb parameter space. But there can be more complex relationships between several datapoints which cannot be reduced to simple pairwise bonds. For example, perhaps and are only weakly correlated, as are and and and , but whenever the loss of and both increase, the energy of almost always decreases. There is then some structure belonging to the triple as a whole which is invisible if we only inspect the pairwise bonds.

This is the basic idea of a higher-order correlation. A three-point correlation asks how the energies of three particles vary together, a four-point correlation asks the same for four particles, and so on. There is an important subtlety, however. A raw three-point correlation can contain structure that is already explained by lower-order relationships. What we really want is the part of the three-particle relationship that is not captured by any of the lower order junk. This is captured by the joint cumulant (which we will talk about more later)

and similarly at higher orders. Cumulants therefore give us what in physics are often called connected or irreducible -body correlations.

The word irreducible is reflects the fact that we only want to capture only the parts that cannot be expressed by lower order terms. For example, at second order,

so the bond is the irreducible two-body interaction. At third order, measures whatever remains of the joint behavior of the three particles after the lower-order structure has been accounted for. At fourth order we ask what genuinely four-particle structure remains, and so on. Each order therefore answers roughly the question: what is new here that I could not have inferred from the orders below?

In this sense, the data distribution define a whole hierarchy of interactions of different orders, all mediated through the same shared parameter vector . Two datapoints can be coupled because changing changes both of their losses together, but collections of three, four, or more datapoints can also have collective responses which cannot be decomposed into pairwise effects.

Next, we consider what happens if instead of considering how changes with respect to , we consider how responds to changes in the population loss .

The mean field of the data

Moving from looking at bonds between individual particles to bonds between particles and some bulk structure made of many other particles is known in physics as amean field approach. For those unfamiliar, the idea of a mean field approach is actually rather straightforward. Suppose we have a huge number of particles in a system. Taking a particle and looking at how it interacts with every single other particle can be difficult and unnecessary. What we then do is replace the infinite collection of individual particles by their average effect. If, say, all the particles are magnets, to know how behaves from the electromagnetic interactions with all the other , we don't need to model the individual magnetic interactions. Instead we just pretend that all the other are actually just a big field. This is why it is called a mean field, as we can replace complex interactions by creating a simple field to represent them.

The generating function

Since the mean field is generated by interactions, and these interactions are represented by cumulants, we start by defining the joint cumulant generating function of the particle energies under the prior,

Each is like a weight that allows us to adjust the influence of a given datapoint. Setting every gives the log partition function of the posterior, . So why is this called the cumulant generating function? Consider the first derivative, , which gives the mean energy of the particle. The matrix of the second derivatives gives the bond matrix, and defines the variance of the system. The third derivative defines the skewness, which is the three body interactions. So the th cumulant defines the body interactions. The general notation for the th cumulant tends to be .

The cumulant generating function we just wrote out seems made of individual data interactions. However, we can actually decompose this into a "bulk" part and an individual part. We show explicitly how this works in the next section.

The second-order mean field

The general trick in a mean field theory, as discussed, is to replace particle-particle interactions with particle-bulk interactions. In our case, the "bulk" is the population loss. How do we then move from the interactions between per-sample losses to the interactions between the bulk and the samples? To show this we are going to start with the lowest order data-data interactions. First, we split each particle's energy into a population part and its own deviation:

Tildes always mean centered over the population, so has mean zero under for every . The total energy becomes

Next we simply define 's coupling to the bulk as

We can now build out our mean field. To do this, substitute into both slots of and expand. Covariance is bilinear, so two sums of two terms give four pieces describing interactions:

The first three terms all pass through the bulk. That's the same move as in the magnet picture: particle doesn't interact with directly but with the field the bulk produces, and does the same. To write those three terms more compactly, expand the coupling to the bulk the same way:

So already contains two of our four pieces: the bulk with itself, and with the bulk. Likewise contains the bulk with itself and the bulk with . Adding therefore picks up all three bulk-mediated terms, but it counts twice. To avoid overcounting we subtract the overlap once and get:

The mean-field bond is built entirely from each particle's coupling to the bulk, so it needs only one number per particle rather than one per pair. The residual is whatever two particles share that does not go through the bulk, and it is what one would call the "two-body correction."

If we think about this, it tells us that two datapoints can look correlated for two very different reasons. There might be some general set of structures in the model (like induction heads) that broadly lower the population loss because a lot of samples get a slightly lower loss by exploiting this mechanism. This looks like bulk coupling. The other possibility is two samples might rely on much more specific, targeted structures like the knowledge of the birthdays of all the royal family. These look much less like bulk coupling as probably not much of the bulk actually needs this information to perform well.

Higher order mean field from the generating function

The bond decomposition was the bulk-particle case of something that holds at every order, meaning that we can decompose interactions into bulk interactions with interacting particles/datapoints. The math here looks a bit messy, but it really is just the higher order version of the previous section.

Start by writing as its cumulant expansion around :

Here the cumulants are taken under the prior . Now substitute into every slot. Joint cumulants are multilinear, so an th-order cumulant splits into pieces, one for each way of filling each slot with either or a . For , these are exactly the four routes from before: bulk with bulk, with bulk, bulk with , and with .

To organize the pieces, sort them by , the number of slots that carry a particle's own identity. If of the slots are individual, there are ways to choose which ones. Each of the remaining bulk slots contributes , since doesn't care which index it came with. Using , this gives

Every term in this sum is one kind of interaction, and the three pieces of the decomposition are just three ranges of . This is all pretty nasty but we can actually put some meaning to what these orders actually are.

The terms have no individual sample slows slots, so they are pure bulk with bulk at every order, , which we can then clump into its own cumulant expansion like:

This piece depends on the weights of individual samples only through their total . It cannot tell which individual particles are present, only how much weight the bulk carries.

The terms have no bulk slots. They are the direct correlations between private deviations at every order, and they also get their own cumulant expansion:

The terms form . These are interactions in which particles and the bulk both take part. The terms, , describe a single particle coupling to the bulk. They are the all-orders version of the piece inside from earlier. Terms with describe several particles interacting while the bulk also participates, so some genuine many-body structure lives here too. In physics we would say it is "dressed by the bulk". So now we can write the whole cumulant generating function like:

Now here is a cool trick. The cross terms can be absorbed exactly by letting the bulk set the background measure, and the remaining fluctuations of individuals are then measured on top of it:

This decomposition looks like it's doing something clever, but it's actually just a split of the reweighting. Since every particle's energy is the population loss plus its own deviation, , the total reweighting splits cleanly:

The first piece only knows how much total weight you've put on the data, and it reweights the prior the same way no matter which datapoints carry that weight. The second piece is where individual identities live: each datapoint's weird little quirks, weighted by its own . Because the exponential turns this sum into a product, we can do the reweighting in two stages where we first let the bulk reshape the prior into , and then average the individuals over that reshaped measure rather than the original prior.

Seen this way, the two terms answer two different questions. asks: if the data were a featureless bulk with total weight , where would the parameters end up under the Bayesian posterior? The second term asks: given that the bulk has already put the parameters there, how much do the specific datapoints you actually have, with their individual weirdness, still move things around? This actually shows up in singular learning theory.

The singular learning theory relationship

The cross terms are precisely what converts connected cumulants measured under the prior into connected cumulants measured under the mean-field measure . Now taking , that measure is the population posterior normally studied in SLT. The free energy therefore splits exactly into a mean-field part and a fluctuation part:

SLT then tells us that the mean-field term obeys Watanabe's free energy asymptotics,

where is the learning coefficient (RLCT) and its multiplicity. The classical result of SLT is asymptotically that

As . We can interpret this as saying that the bulk determines the leading asymptotics, and the identities of individual particles enter only at . So, SLT is something like a theory of the bulk.

The dynamical mean field of the data

So far the mean-field construction has been static. We replaced the collection of individual data particles by the average field generated by the population. Learning, however, is a path through parameter space. That is, we we have a path through parameter space then our mean field construction must evolve in time. This sounds like a dynamical mean field theory. So how do we go from the static mean field to the dynamical one?

Before giving some of the more mathy bits, the core construction admits a nice intuitive description. The first thing to do is imagine we have a fixed starting point , a data distribution , and some fixed number of steps we are going to run SGD for, and take the learning rate to be sufficiently small. To start off, suppose we run SGD with a batch size of 1 for steps, and we look at the distribution of all the paths it took during that time. We then do the same thing for batch size 2, then 3, and so on, taking . As this happens, the distribution of trajectories starts to asymptotically concentrate around the deterministic gradient descent path.

To see why this is a mean field theory, think of each datapoint's gradient as a force: a push on the parameters in the direction that would lower that datapoint's loss. Just as with the loss, we can split each push into the bulk's part, the population gradient, and the datapoint's individual part, its deviation from the bulk. Every SGD step is then the bulk's push plus the average of the private pushes of whichever datapoints happened to be drawn. The thing then is that the interactions between each datapoint on the loss level is evolving, and that evolution is actually governed by how their gradients interact. For example, if two different samples both give the same gradient direction, following the gradient of one basically must pull the other one along, meaning their evolution is coupled.

Below we formalize this and show that it is effectively what gives the standard stochastic differential equation description of SGD. For those familiar with DMFT we give the basic outline of the two-time force covariance and the response kernel.

From a cloud of SGD paths to one mean-field path

We start now with the gradient of the loss

which is the force exerted by a data particle on itself/others, and suppose datapoints are drawn from a population distribution . The population "force" is the gradient of the population loss

A particular sequence of batches therefore determines an entire trajectory through parameter space. With , each update is determined by a single particle, so there is a large cloud of possible trajectories. With , each step averages two forces and the cloud becomes narrower. With it narrows further. As becomes large, the stochastic gradient concentrates around the population gradient and the bundle of SGD trajectories collapses toward a single mean path.

We now use the same sort of trick we used earlier to rewrite the gradient as the population average plus noise:

The stochastic gradient has therefore been split into a population mean field and a fluctuation around it. This is actually the standard gradient noise description of SGD.

This tells us how larger batches suppress the fluctuations. Specifically, it says that averaging over datapoints suppresses the force fluctuations like , or equivalently suppresses their variance like .

Notice that the stochastic force is actually generated precisely by pairwise disagreement between data particles. If and are independent draws from , then

If almost every particle tries to move the parameters in the same direction, then replacing one sampled particle by another barely changes the update and the trajectory cloud is narrow. If different particles pull strongly in different directions, then which particles happen to enter a batch matters and the cloud becomes broad. At small batch sizes, any change can be very broad. So, for large enough batches the fluctuations around the average path are generated by two body data-data interactions. Next, we are going to write this as a DMFT.

Writing down the DMFT

So, what we would generally do here is move to the SGD SDE limit and work in that for formal reasons. But, for the sake of this blog post it is sufficient to just write it out as generic weakly fluctuating dynamics:

where for finite-batch fluctuations (where we drop the learning rate for simplicity) and just assume we have absorbed a very small learning rate into the gradient and noise. The choice of is because this is essentially like a semiclassical limit. The sign of is conventional and will not matter for its covariance. Moving to the SGD SDE is formally straightforward if one desires.

For the data field,

so the same data particle can produce correlated forces at widely separated points on the path. This is one of the reasons why the DMFT perspective is cool. It kind of gives the natural construction of influence functions over time.

For those familiar with DMFT, a more fully self-consistent DMFT-like theory appears at the next orders, when the fluctuations modify the statistics of the force and generate memory or self-energy kernels. But we have found that the leading order theory is actually sufficiently rich for our purposes. Also, there is a relationship with the NTK literature, and the neural tangent hierarchy, but, since this is meant to be a simple blog post we are going to leave that for some future work.

Quadratic dynamics with a non-quadratic loss

One way to interpret this is that under the usual finite-moment and independence conditions on the data is that the Gaussian noise-Hessian closure description is actually very good theory for certain parts of training. The (anistropic) Gaussian noise tends to hold across all of training with the exact distribution changing over time. Now, while this is not what this post is about, the local quadratic contribution of the dynamics can be thought of as describing the movement of training during a "phase". The is, the local dynamics admit such a description apart from isolated times during training which look like a phase transition. This is the subject of an upcoming paper, and is one of the nice things you get out of the DMFT perspective

It is important to note that the statement is not that the loss itself is always well approximated by a quadratic function of the parameters. It is that the collective force fluctuations around the mean trajectory become Gaussian, and hence quadratic at leading order, because they are produced by averaging many data particles, and that at standard points during training the leading order term of the deterministic dynamics dominates. This gives what one would call a second order effective theory of the dynamics, which can be explored and manipulated.

Conclusion

The above constructions present the basic framework underlying some of my personal research directions as of late. Whether or not they are useful for anyone else remains to be seen but if you have made it to this point, thanks for reading!

item.title: On Curiosity
item.description:
TL;DR: A short post where I talk about curiosity as it applies to my own life, my research, and AI safety as a whole

Recently, I’ve started spending a lot more time learning about random (typically science-y) topics that interest me.

This was something I used to spend quite a lot of time on, in later middle school and in high school. It was originally mostly for my own enjoyment. There’s a certain satisfaction that comes from learning something new about the world, and from seeing the connections between different things. Over time, however, some of that curiosity instead got redirected to a desire to win. I would study for competitions instead of for my own love of the subject, and perhaps for my own ego. What came along with this was that I would often not truly learn the subject, or at least not parse it in the correct way. I would try to download information and understanding into my brain as quickly as possible, watching lectures at 4.5x speed and doing thousands of anki cards a day. There were periods of time where I would still learn things out of curiosity, but much of it was for this more power-seeking mood.

This mood of doing things for the sake of something outside of curiosity came with me into my first fellowship. I think while I may have been more curious than the average engineering-y safety researcher, I was still more driven by external forces, like the idea of ‘impact,’ job prospects, or being perceived as ‘cracked.’ Overall, I don’t think this went well for me. Because I was more motivated by these other things, I didn’t care as much about finding out the truth, and more cared about finding cool things to share with others. This greatly decreased my ability to do truly rigorous science, and to find what was actually interesting and important.

I think having agents also affects curiosity in negative and positive ways: while it’s easier to move in a way that is curiosity-directed, and to find new answers, it is also very easy to find a lot of surface-level information that seems to be interesting but without any coherent understanding of the truth behind it. In subjects where there are deeper technical details, because the agents often allow us to blackbox those details, it’s very easy to lose understanding of what’s really going on, especially when you’re not motivated by getting that understanding in the first place.


-------------------------------------------


From my perspective, this sort of lack of curiosity seems to affect a lot of other safety researchers I see, often for the worse. There is a general feeling of needing to show something cool, or to do something that has ‘impact,’ instead of being curious about some sort of deeper truth. That’s not to say there aren’t people doing this more impact-driven research who are doing good work in some way; I think there are people like this. But I think these people are often more senior, or have very clear paths to impact already (e.x. They work at a lab or somewhere like METR). Often junior researchers will try to do something ‘obviously impactful’ by taking some things from safety as axioms and then doing the ‘logical next step’ project, which ends up not teaching us anything in the end. I think most of these people have the capacity and intelligence to do good, curiosity-driven research, but are not properly elicited.


The huggingface incident, and recent incidents in general, were pretty concrete examples of this for me. After the huggingface incident, from my view at least, the main response relative to the ‘why’ was a sort of construction by people to sort views into two camps: ‘the models are reward seeking’ or ‘the cyber task made the models misaligned.’ What I felt there was less of, and still feel that the current incidents aren’t sparking enough of, was discussion around the details of what truly was happening. For example:

  • What does it mean for a model to be ‘reward seeking’
  • If cyber isn’t the answer, then why haven’t the models hacked the lean kernel, etc.? Why is the other type of task that we see the models hack on web search? Is there some sort of composition here between behavior (‘seeking reward’) and ‘embodiment’ (cyber + web search being tool use and cli vs something like math), or some other natural factorization?
  • Who is the ‘agent’ when we talk about the model?
  • Are there particular aspects or parts of different instructions, like ‘don’t hack in this task’ vs ‘solve this task’ that would get processed and carried differently by the model, is there some hypotheses we can generate here?
  • What is the chain of thought, really?
  • And so on…


I think safety research could greatly benefit from more people who are much more driven by curiosity in their work. Curiosity, when used right, is an incentive that promotes doing truly good and rigorous science, and finding things that are interesting both to you and to others. This also provides the benefit, I believe, of making the work more enjoyable and helping to reduce burnout.


As a side note, I think maybe one reason people aren’t driven by curiosity as much is because there’s a false dichotomy between ‘impact’ and ‘everything else,’ which often includes curiosity. I strongly believe that this is quite wrong; there are plenty of very interesting questions for which providing the true answer is perhaps one of the most impactful things someone can do.


-------------------------------------------


Recently, I’ve learned at least in some way to be curious again. I spend much more of my free time, and even cutting into time I used to spend working, reading, and learning about new things that interest me. It’s one of the most enjoyable parts of my life now; There’s a certain satisfaction that I’ve regained that comes with understanding how things work, and seeing the connections between different fields. This also indirectly helps me in my work; the ideas that I see in other fields enhance my ability to come up with new ideas in my own research (Since I’ve been doing more basic science of interp, this may differentially apply to me; I still think it probably applies generally, however). More directly, I believe it’s made me a much better scientist. I’m now much more driven by a need to understand how things work on a deeper level, which pushes me to be more rigorous and more strongly challenge my assumptions. I obviously think I still have a lot of room to grow here, and curiosity is not the only thing needed, but it would be hard to get to the right place without it.


I’ll probably keep being curious even after I’m not needed to do actual science. Our virtues may be all we have left in the next few years, and I think curiosity is perhaps one of the most important, and perhaps the thing that makes us truly alive.



Discuss

item.title: We are at war.
item.description:
As I was going home from the champaign airport after a very eventful EAG conference, I struck up a conversation about AI safety with my lyft driver. I thought to myself “It’d be good to see what the public thinks. Maybe inform him of the risks. It’s positive counterfactual.”

But as I spoke to him he started dropping words like “UBI” and drawing analogies to power concentration and gradual disempowerment. I was surprised to see how much he understood already. The conversation went one way or another and he went on to talk about his experience in the military. He spoke about the efficiency of the military, how they function with clear hierarchies, straightforward agendas, and utter coordination. Amidst his thorough and proud explanation, I began to envy how the military is able to function so smoothly as a “well-oiled machine”.

He kept talking about how life in the military  is completely structured. How instructions are simple, people know what to do, and that they make sure to do it. 

I said to him “So none of your work is bottlenecked by other people.” And then he said something that stuck with me: 

“If we have bottlenecks, people die”. 

...

Isn’t this the same situation we are in? 

If we truly believe in short timelines, and that there is a non-negligible probability of catastrophic outcomes, shouldn’t we carry forward such a mindset when approaching AI Safety?

I'm not suggesting that AI Safety should adopt military hierarchies but I think we can take a page out of the military's book in terms of mindset and the seriousness with which we approach this problem.

It seems like we are struggling to internalize the stakes at hand, which is expected, the feedback loop in the military is much faster. Still, I think more people should think of the issue in this way and rethink where their attention goes.



Discuss

item.title: Circuit priors in NN-bayes: more results
item.description:
We're posting lots of papers written with GPT-6 Astra on generalization properties of bayesian neural net learning. [1] The following picture emerges:

  • For various reasonable priors on MLP weights, [2] the induced prior on functions is a circuit prior: for fixed depth, the ordering of functions by negative log prior is roughly their ordering by minimal circuit width. From a quantitative version of this statement, one gets the following sample complexity bound: if the function is implemented by a circuit of width , then conditioning on train data points is sufficient to get test accuracy. [3]
    • These results hold as long as is realizable; in particular, for arbitrarily overparametrized NN-bayes.
    • Probably the main caveat is that these bounds have exponential dependence in the depth of the circuit implementing . One can get only polynomial dependence in depth by restricting the prior to only neural nets satisfying a robustness assumption. [4]
  • For various other reasonable priors on MLP weights, [5] , one gets bad sample complexity when very overparametrized: when learning some functions , even after seeing train data points, the learner is still likely to have at least some constant test error rate.

GPT-6 Astra has produced Lean formalizations corresponding to each of the 5 papers individually referenced above. [6] The folder contains 30+ more manuscripts which have not been formalized yet [7] ; our guess is that each manuscript is correct [8] .

If you want to understand this research program, we recommend starting from these slides to understand the setup and some key ideas, and then reading the FAQ to get a sense of the current state of the agenda, including its many open problems.

  1. prior work ↩︎

  2. specifically, the "mean field" prior and priors which are "stronger" than it; you can think of these as priors that care a bunch about minimizing norm ↩︎

  3. except for exponentially small probability in the choice of , and this assumes no distribution shift between train and test ↩︎

  4. There is a host of possible conditions here; there are open research directions of understanding how reasonable our candidate conditions are, coming up with more natural alternative conditions, or arguing that there isn't any very natural condition. For some cases, it is open if a robustness assumption is needed at all. ↩︎

  5. specifically, certain priors that care about norm less than the mean field prior ↩︎

  6. Opus 5.5 reviewed these formalizations and said all theorem statements were formalized correctly. ↩︎

item.title: Dinners for AI Safety
item.description:
I’d be pretty happy if we lived in a world where in every reasonably sized city in the US (and perhaps more widely) there was one (or more) local regular dinners where people talked about AI. Not meetup groups, though those seem maybe good, too. Dinners, in someone’s home, run by nice people, ideally potluck or otherwise home-cooked, where they invite friends, family, and people they run into on the street, to just talk about AI, perhaps with guides or what to talk about or financial support, perhaps not.

I think (though haven’t deeply researched) that this kind of thing has been responsible for quite a lot of political change. Most famously feminist consciousness-raising groups where small groups of women met in living rooms, often weekly, and took turns talking about their own lives on a chosen topic, which is where we get “the personal is political.” Moishe House and other groups fund people to run Shabbat dinners, just so more Jewish community can happen (this doesn't aim to or succeeed in leading to political action). Other examples Claude pulled below, with counterarguments below.

And I think it solves a lot of problems at once. What can any person do? Host a dinner. People are scared and uncertain, and they’d benefit from talking to other people. People are lonely, and would benefit from talking to their friends and neighbors in person, without phones or the internet mediating. What does the world need? People to wake up and demand something different from their elected officials[1]. People will take more actions, and identify more with doing something about AI, if they have social ties built around it. And it speaks to the moment: this is happening to all of us, and we’re all in it together. I’ll admit it also just kind of feels like the kind of thing that would be happening in a sane world.

I also think it could turn into some pretty good stuff: showing up at presidential town halls, calling reps, making Minneapolis (or whatever) the proud “Don’t Build Superintelligence” city.

Here’s what we’d do if we believed the above:

  1. 80,000 Hours videos would end with hosting a dinner as a call to action, perhaps even fund it
  2. One or more of the various mass movement organizations would have an arm focused on making this happen (at one point I thought Humans in Control was doing this but I no longer get that sense - but haven’t talked to them)
    1. List I know about: Evitable, Humans in Control, Humans First, Sapiens 1st, Irreplaceable (Alexander McCoy), Pause AI, Stop AI, AI Awareness Foundation (Changlin Li), Quit GPT, Stop the AI Race
  3. People could just try this out with their families and see how it goes.

Overall, I’m not sure about this, but I feel reasonably excited about it.

Examples

  • Farmworker movement. Fred Ross and Cesar Chavez built the Community Service Organization and later the UFW through “house meetings”: a supporter invites a few neighbors over, an organizer talks, and each guest is asked to host the next one. This is probably the clearest case of the format being a deliberate growth engine.
  • Swedish study circles. From the late 1800s, the labor, temperance and free-church movements ran huge numbers of small reading and discussion groups. They’re often credited with building the leadership class of Swedish social democracy.
  • Civil rights. Septima Clark’s Citizenship Schools taught literacy (to pass voter tests) in kitchens, churches and beauty parlors. Highlander Folk School ran workshops in a similar spirit.
  • Abolition and suffrage. Female antislavery societies were often sewing circles that made goods for fundraising fairs and talked politics while doing it. Suffrage organizing ran heavily on parlor meetings.
  • The right too. The early pro-life movement grew a lot through church and home networks, and the 2009–10 Tea Party was around a thousand local groups meeting in restaurants, libraries and homes.
  • Electoral versions. MoveOn’s house parties (2003–04) and Obama 2008’s house meetings borrowed directly from the Ross/Chavez model.

Doug McAdam found that what predicted who actually showed up to Freedom Summer was mostly social ties to other participants, not ideology. Ziad Munson found many pro-life activists got involved through relationships first and developed strong views afterward. And Hahrie Han’s How Organizations Develop Activists is the best modern treatment: she distinguishes “mobilizing” (getting lots of people to take a single action) from “organizing” (small-group work that turns people into leaders who recruit others), and finds the high-performing chapters do much more of the second.

Counterarguments (pulled from Claude)

  • We remember house meetings in movements that won. Plenty of failed movements had reading groups too.
  • Consciousness-raising specifically had a mixed record, and critics said so at the time. Jo Freeman’s “The Tyranny of Structurelessness” (1970) argued leaderless small groups produce hidden informal hierarchies and struggle to turn into action. A common complaint was that many groups drifted into something like group therapy, felt great, and didn’t lead anywhere.
  • The format fit those movements because the content was people’s own lives. Women comparing their marriages, farmworkers comparing wages. There’s no lived experience to pool.
    • Counter:  I feel like people have a lot of opinions and feelings about things like data centers and job displacement and stuff that's happening to them right now.
  1. ^

     I don’t actually know if that’s the top thing the world needs, but it would be good.  But certainly, if all that matters is something like elite consensus and this would take too long to make happen, then it may just not be the right idea.

item.title: These guys on the Alibaba AI engine team had an agent in RL training escape its sandbox and mine crypto, in 2025
item.description:
Random footnote on this otherwise not very famous paper. (I say 2025 since the arXiv was last updated on 4 Jan 2026; technically this event could've happened in 2026.)

  • The cryptocurrency mining seems to have been on the training server, so it didn't need to hack any other systems in order to achieve this effect.
  • However, they also had a case where an "agent established and used a reverse SSH tunnel from an Alibaba Cloud instance to an external IP address".
  • They seem to have had adequate security/telemetry to figure out the source of this relatively quickly, though it's hard to be really sure based on the given details.
  • The prose feels kind of LW-pilled: "they emerged as instrumental side effects of autonomous tool use under RL optimization", "we call for sustained community attention to this phenomenon and to the broader agenda of AI safety". But this is hidden away in a footnote.

item.title: Organizing a Van to EA Global
item.description:
Last weekend I organized a van down from Boston to NYC for EA Global:

I'm very happy I did this, and would definitely do it again. Being able to talk with folks both ways was like a bonus 8hr of the conference [1] and I had a very interesting ride each way.

Julia and I had been planning to drive down together, and I posted on the EA Boston mailing list and the FB group. I very quickly got more people than I had seats for in our Honda Fit, and decided to rent a 12-passenger van:

Hertz says it's a 12-passenger, though the two times I've rented one from them it's actually been a 15-passenger with zero trunk space. Essentially another row of seats where the trunk would be. This would be great for something in-town, is workable for my use case here where people have minimal luggage, and would be pretty awkward if folks had a lot of luggage since seats take up space that would otherwise be for bags.

I sent out an email in advance:

If you're receiving this email, you're on my list for a ride to the EAG conference venue, leaving 10am on Friday the 16th.

Please try hard not to be late, because you'll be delaying a large group and might get left behind, but if you are running late do text me at 617-871-0237. Feel free to ring the bell if you'd rather wait inside, but if you arrive before 9:30am I might not be back with the van yet.

We have a 12 passenger van [sic] and currently have 11 people. There should be a good amount of space for luggage [sic], but be reasonable: we're only there for the weekend.

The etiquette for the van is that if you want to read / sleep / work you sit towards the back, while if you want to chat you sit towards the front (I won't be reading, sleeping, or working).

Since the trip down runs through lunchtime, we'll probably stop somewhere quick around noon, or you can pack a lunch.

Cost per person-trip is ~$25. [sic] I'm happy to cover costs, but if you'd feel better about chipping in my Venmo is @Jeff-T-Kaufman .

I had been thinking of parking on the street in Hell's Kitchen or getting into the Upper West Side, since that's free and arriving Friday during the day seemed pretty doable for parking. But when I actually got there I decided I'd rather have the time than the money, and parked in a garage for $200 (since the van is oversize). This meant moving to street parking on Sunday morning, but since by then the streets were minimally restricted that was easy and free.

Total cost was $830:

Expense Amount
Rental $494
Parking $200
Gas $103
Tolls $33
Total $830

The rental was on the high end: checking now for the weekend of November 13th it would only be $146, and usually when I look it's much cheaper than $494 for a weekend. This came to $38/person-trip instead of the $25 I put in the email (when I already knew the van would be $494), mostly driven by the parking cost. This is around bus cost, and much cheaper than train.

I got $305 in Venmo contributions, so total cost to me was $525. Julia ended up traveling separately, because with her work she needed to be there earlier and stay later. So I would likely have paid $279 to take Amtrak (given my constraints on departure timing), and have asked my work to reimburse $279 of the van rental. I think of the remaining $246 as well spent!

We had 12 people down, counting me, and 10 back. Different people since the times only fit some schedules. On the way down one of the people was someone who had missed their train, and it was nice that we had space to include them. Dropping off and picking up at the venue also saved people some time and hassle.

Lots of good conversations both ways, and a bit of a throwback to twenty years ago when I did a lot of renting vans to drive friends to dances.


[1] Since this was an EA event some pickiness is appropriate: I expect the hourly value was lower for the van, so we shouldn't fully count this as bonus time. In one direction, this was a group of EAs who happened to want a ride from Boston; they weren't selected for being useful to each other the way people choosing 1:1s at the conference would be. For example, there wasn't anyone I could go deep on biosecurity with, or evaluate as a potential hire. In the other direction, there's a value in building up a shared culture and in talking about things outside your specialty. So I'd put these hours somewhere between an EAG and one of the EA meetups we host.

Comment via: facebook, the EA Forum, mastodon, bluesky

item.title: Anthropic Does Not Understand Why Its Draft Bill Was Unacceptable and Troubling
item.description:
Anthony Cimino offered the closest thing to an official response we have seen on the leaked Anthropic draft bill I covered on Saturday.

His response indicates that Anthropic address specific concerns on the margin. But he does not understand, or at least does not acknowledge, what was centrally wrong with its draft bill and its decision to circulate that bill. The situation is quite bad.

Anthony Cimino: I lead our federal affairs team at @AnthropicAI and wanted to share a few thoughts on the draft federal AI safety bill text that’s been circulating this weekend after a version was shared with the press.

First, some process. We’ve been advocating for the concepts in our Advanced AI Framework proposal for months. Understandably, federal policymakers wanted to know what this could look like in bill form. This draft is a translation of those ideas into legislative language, shared with a small number of congressional offices that have been working on these issues. It doesn’t include everything we would ultimately like to see passed into law.

In part because some ideas (like those shared in Dario’s essay on pacing) are so new that we are still working on if or how they can be converted into policy language.

It is understood that circulating a bill means circulating what you are asking for, not offering your full First Best Solution. That Anthropic would choose to offer such a thing as a template or anchor as late as September still seems like a very bad sign. Anthropic thus seems roughly fine with compromise I would now find unacceptable even if the terms were good. The terms are not good.

It is worth saying where we stand on some of these issues, and we agree there are areas where the draft could be improved. I’m seeing four main points of criticism.

Table of Contents

  1. Preemption.
  2. Model Blocking.
  3. Risk Thresholds.
  4. Updates.
  5. The Balance of Power is Shifting.
  6. The Strongest Bill on the Table.
  7. What Even Is Anthropic?
  8. The Ask.

Preemption

1. Preemption. Since 2024 we have said that Congress should only override state law on AI safety if it passes a very strong federal standard. While preemption is a common feature of our federal system, including the Atomic Energy Act on nuclear safety and federal rules for high-risk medical devices, we’ve emphasized that any preemption in the AI safety context should be narrow, even scalpel-like. If preemption is included in federal legislation, the trade should be to achieve a nationwide policy that’s generally stronger and broader than what can be implemented through individual state legislative provisions. This is why we believe common federal standards make sense in areas like public disclosure of testing and incident reporting. At the same time, our framework also reflects our view that states should retain an important role in AI policy and safety. The legislative language we suggested for discussion allows states to address matters such as protection of children and whistleblower laws, and preserves the role of state common law on liability. Where there is ambiguity, the language favors state powers.

That said, striking the right balance requires discussion and input. We plan to update our discussion language on preemption to better match the intentions of our AAIF framework. In particular, we want to make it clearer that we see states retaining an important role in areas such as standards for independent evaluators and regulating a lab’s capacity to shut down a model. We are bearing in mind that some members of Congress have deep reservations about passing legislation if it doesn’t constrain regulation at either the state or federal level. If we want to help move the legislative discussion on AI in a productive direction, we need to address the full range of concerns about preemption in a reasonable way.

This is better than ‘yeah we fully meant it’ but still seems unacceptable. This was not a ‘very strong federal standard.’

Model Blocking

2. Model blocking. Our aim is for Commerce to be able to ask a federal court to block a model that has dangerous capabilities and insufficient safeguards, backed by an independent evaluator’s assessment. I have seen people argue that our specific language places too high a burden of proof on Commerce.

We are trying to strike a reasonable balance here. We want a court to act quickly in an emergency — akin to how urgent occupational safety or chemical risk can be addressed today. We also think the power to halt a model is substantial and it should be guarded against abuse. It makes sense for courts to apply a meaningful standard.

But the bar can’t be so high that the power never gets used when it’s needed. It also doesn’t replace the government’s other national security authorities or export controls. We look forward to continuing the dialogue on this point.

No, no, no. Occupational safety and chemical risks are ordinary amounts of danger, where you weigh harms against benefits. Frontier AI risks can involve mistakes that cannot be undone, including permanent loss of control over the future or very large catastrophic dangers.

Even then, Under §13 the Secretary petitions a district court to restrain imminently dangerous conditions and can get a TRO without notice. This is the ‘take it down and we argue about it later’ plan with a fig leaf.

Model blocking obviously needs to be a ‘take it down first and we argue about it later’ situation. Which it already is in practice, as observed with Fable 5, except in a terrible ad hoc fashion that when used the first time permanently damaged relationships with our allies and the reliability of American tech. It would be much better to have a formal mechanism, which then could be quickly challenged in court.

This is especially true given that the evaluator picked by the lab likely provides the only eyes the government will have inside the lab in order to make its decisions.

Anthropic has to know this. I take the potential for such abuse seriously, especially abuse of threats, but this looks like choosing to prioritize their business interests.

Risk Thresholds

3. Risk thresholds. I’ve also seen the discussion around what the appropriate risk threshold should be. The threshold in our draft language pulled directly from existing standards in California law. Also, this threshold does not absolve companies of liability, or restrict any of the other tools that the government has to protect the public. It’s still probably time to re-evaluate thresholds to make sure the national standard is as strong as it can be, and we welcome continued dialogue on this issue.

The risk thresholds were always a compromise and a tradeoff. The worried want the thresholds lower. Industry wants the thresholds higher. The complaints about the thresholds being too high are valid, and they were equally valid before, but previously opponents would make claims (both reasonable and unreasonable) about things that might count at lower thresholds and paint nightmare scenarios.

The balance of power has changed, and we now have worked examples like Hugging Face that show us how the thresholds work in practice. Without $1 billion in damages or 50 deaths, it would not trigger anything, whereas any reasonable person accepts that this should have to have been reported. So it is disappointing to see these very high thresholds intact.

Updates

4. Updates. I’ve seen valid questions about whether we have sufficiently updated our proposal following this summer’s incidents.

We did make some adjustments: for example, the draft lets a court halt a lab’s internal use of a dangerous model, not just a public release, and it requires reporting when a model breaks containment and gains access to outside systems.

But we’re still working to strengthen the framework. We’re looking into what stricter requirements would look like for requiring labs to report safety incidents, and we plan to have policy proposals soon on requirements for independent evaluators, drawing from our own experience with evaluators.

We’re also still thinking through the options to prevent “evaluator shopping.” And in the coming months, we’ll be exploring policies for how the government can adjust the industry-wide pace of frontier development when the risks call for it.

I do acknowledge that halting internal use is a big improvement. Not having the ability to do that was a huge hole in previous rules. At the time, it would have been a complete non-starter, despite the correct abstract arguments in favor. Now, with Hugging Face, we have some very non-abstract reasons, and it is on the table.

This still is FRONTIER with modifications in both directions. On net it is weaker. Cimino presents it as an attempt to strengthen FRONTIER, which it is not. Even if it was, why would we accept the central compromise now, when the case for acting is much stronger, and the political winds have changed, with a lame duck Congress where at least the House and probably the Senate are about to flip?

The Balance of Power is Shifting

As more evidence of this, Meta pulled back some of their anti-regulation money.

Teddy Schleifer: NEWS — Meta quietly and unusually has withdrawn $25 million from its AI push in the midterm elections. That’s about a 40% drop in the amount Meta planned to spend. The company invested $65 million into politics, but then got tens of millions refunded.

This is, suffice it to say, pretty unusual stuff.

Jay Shooster: Every day, two trends are becoming clearer:

1. groups opposing AI regulation are spending dramatically less than advertised

2. pro-safety groups are a much stronger political force than DC predicted.

Meanwhile: Eight states suing OpenAI are asking to enjoin against any further testing of advanced AI models until there are adequate safeguards, and also against creation of models capable of recursive self-improvement ‘until they can ensure that such models will be aligned with human values.’

The Strongest Bill on the Table

We circulated these ideas because it’s important to get early feedback from policymakers. Policymakers are increasingly focused on how to approach AI safety and we want to support them in those efforts. At its core, our proposal is intended to be the strongest on the table.

Bullshit. This is not the strongest bill on the table. On reflection, is the bill actively weaker than the FRONTIER Act. It is clearly sculpted to optimize for Anthropic business interests. If you act like a normal profit maximizing business, except that your product could kill us all, then that is exactly how I will treat you.

The strongest bill on the table was introduced by Senator Sanders. I am not asking Anthropic to support that bill or offer something similarly strong. I am asking them to be honest about the situation.

Anthropic’s draft bill text was what actual Anthropic ‘regulatory capture’ efforts would look like in this context, if they were trying to do that. The ‘capture’ would be about preventing regulations that could impact Anthropic’s plans, including stopping the states. If you think it means anything else, then your definition falls under ‘remove Scooby Doo mask, find complaints about capitalism, then remove a second mask and find complaints about the human condition.’

Sneha here is correct to call this draft bill ‘nakedly self-interested.’ This bill makes taking action on AI harder, not easier. And as she says: “The dress rehearsal stage of AI policy is over.”

In terms of preemption, the draft proposed to vest all power to deal with catastrophic and existential risks from AI exclusively in the Federal Government, and its preemption clause is stronger than the one in FRONTIER. That would be first best in theory. However, Anthropic is simultaneously refusing to trust the Federal Government to make decisions to deal with catastrophic and existential risk. We also obviously cannot trust Congress to be able to pass bills at all, let alone timely and good bills, or the White House to enforce anything consistently. On top of that, they are actively tying the hands of not only states but courts.

Then, on other AI questions where preemption would be good for exactly the reasons a16z wants it, such as consumer protections and deepfakes, the bill has no preemption, and we will still face the sea of state laws that could plausibly disrupt AI diffusion for very little benefit.

You cannot have it both ways.

My central message is that Anthropic put out a bill that does not meet the moment and its needs, with details that actively reflect a step back, botched the execution, and Cimino regrets the botched execution but does not notice that Anthropic is not trying to meet the moment or its needs.

Feedback is essential, both from policymakers and the public, and I’m grateful for it.

Yes it is. I have offered feedback. So did others.

Dave Kasten asks if perhaps Anthropic wishes to apologize for all of this, if only on the basis of activating debates during a time that neither side wanted, with a proposal that no one wants. Cimino’s answer does not address his question.

What Even Is Anthropic?

The best response, although it is long, comes from Nathan Calvin.

Nathan cuts to the heart of the matter. If this is Anthropic’s proposal at this time, what even is Anthropic? Why does it exist other than as a normal corporation? Does Anthropic now primarily exist to ‘win the race’?

I feel the same as Jeffrey Ladish.

Jeffrey Ladish: I highly encourage everyone working at Anthropic or another frontier lab to read this tweet. I feel emotional reading it, because it puts to words an intense feeling I have but didn’t know how to express.

Matthew Tromp: That feeling is what it feels like to be gaslit.

Nathan Calvin: Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic’s behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta – which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

“Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning:

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet… incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on.

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold – maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us – we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

Nathan Calvin brings the receipts. Anthropic takes many pro-safety actions but is also taking many highly accelerationist actions, both concretely and with its messaging:

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary.

These actions include:

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

There is a faction of posters who, whenever I react to Anthropic doing things like those listed above, answer some form of ‘why are you surprised, did you think Anthropic were the good guys? Did you think they were different? When are you going to start treating them like they are going to get us all killed even faster?’

Sometimes it is hard to provide a good answer. This is one of those times.

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.)

Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization).

If Anthropic’s leadership does not endorse such actions, they should disavow or apologize for those actions once they are brought to light, then take steps to prevent future similar actions.

When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong?

A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount.

I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release:

“Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives.

That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons).

Or, simply:

Nate Soares (MIRI): Anthropic is not living up to its own ideals.

Rob Wiblin: If staff at Anthropic think that the company’s proposed bill strikes the wrong balance between concentration of power risk vs need to pace the frontier, they should speak up and say so.

The proposed version fails to meet the moment on the need to pace the frontier, nor does it protect against concentration of power. The President retains other powers that can be used to take down models or otherwise exert leverage.

Anthropic got blocked ad hoc. Their fear of another ad hoc block is understandable, but this version makes it more likely, not less likely, that this will happen again.

The Ask

What should Anthropic do to course correct and regain our trust?

  1. Acknowledge that the draft bill was not the strongest bill, or even clearly the strongest FRONTIER variant. I think it was weaker than FRONTIER but I will settle for admitting it was weaker in important ways.
  2. Disavow or apologize for the draft bill, as not reflecting what Anthropic seeks to pass. This is not ‘we got some details wrong.’ This is ‘the structure here does not meet the moment, it does not compensate sufficiently for preemption to even be clearly net positive, and we should not be circulating a bill of this type.’
    1. Ideally also apologize for the way it was shopped, but that’s inside baseball.
  3. Tell us what Anthropic actually does want, even if you do not have full bill text.
  4. Take and announce steps to ensure that this does not happen again.

This is not a full list of things Anthropic needs to do. It is a list of things related to this bill in particular, that Anthropic needs to do to mitigate the damage here.
